extracted.intended_audience: Catholic educators, clergy, university founders, and others interested in the aims and principles of university (liberal) education (mid-19th century context)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and practical guidance about the nature, aims, curriculum, and governance of a university (especially a Catholic university), focusing on formation of the intellect and the institutional role of teaching versus research.

rubrics_metrics.name: University defined as a place of teaching universal knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “That it is a place of teaching universal knowledge. This implies that its object is, on the one hand, intellectual, not moral; and, on the other, that it is the diffusion and extension of knowledge rather than the advancement.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and implications: if the object were scientific/philosophical discovery, the author argues, a university would not need students; the university's primary office is intellectual education and diffusion of knowledge to students rather than original discovery. (Anti-pattern: treating a university primarily as a research academy.)

rubrics_metrics.name: University's object is intellectual (not moral) and directed to students
rubrics_metrics.description: The university's object is, on the one hand, intellectual, not moral; and, on the other, the diffusion and extension of knowledge rather than the advancement. 'If religious training, I do not see how it can be the seat of literature and science.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize intellectual instruction over moral or narrowly religious aims when defining the University's proper office; while religion may relate, it should not supplant the university's intellectual character. (Scoring note: programs or policies that prioritize vocational or sectarian moral formation over broad intellectual instruction depart from this standard.)

rubrics_metrics.name: The Church's role: necessary for the University's integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Practically speaking, [a University] cannot fulfil its object duly ... without the Church's assistance; or, to use the theological term, the Church is necessary for its integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Church does not change the University's main character as an intellectual institution but steadies it in performance and secures spiritual welfare of its students. Guidance includes adapting university formation to serve the Church's pastoral/spiritual ends (e.g., educating Catholics in a Catholic form) without converting the university into an exclusively religious seminary. (Example: establishing a Catholic University to give Catholics the same advantages Protestant institutions provide, but in a Catholic form.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of intellectual labour: Universities teach, Academies research
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Universit[ies] are established for teaching the sciences to the pupils who wish to be formed; the Academies propose new researches to be made in the course of the sciences.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat teaching and discovery as distinct institutional functions and gifts; do not expect the same persons or institutions to excel equally at both. Historical examples: Plato, Aristotle, Newton, great discoverers often worked in seclusion and were not primarily public lecturers. (Anti-pattern: designing a university as if it must primarily be a research institute that also trains students.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary aim: cultivation and formation of the intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: The advantages to be given by a University are 'the culture of the intellect' — force, steadiness, comprehensiveness, versatility, command over our own powers, and the instinctive just estimate of things as they pass before us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success by the extent to which students gain intellectual steadiness, consistency of view, good sense, candour, self-command, and the capacity to enter any subject of thought with aptitude. (Examples: avoiding flippancy, prejudice, and inconsistent opinion; producing citizens capable of public and professional duties.)

rubrics_metrics.name: University curriculum should discipline the mind: sequence and content
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The first step in intellectual training is to impress upon a boy’s mind the idea of science, method, order, principle, and system… This is commonly and excellently done by making him begin with Grammar… A second science is the Mathematics: this should follow Grammar… Hence, too, Chronology and Geography… Metrical Composition when he reads Poetry…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical sequence: begin with grammar (precision of language and critical scholarship), follow with mathematics (conception of development and arrangement), then chronology/geography (for history), and include metrical composition for poetry to stimulate active powers. Emphasize accuracy, minuteness, and critical scholarship as disciplinary tools. (Scoring note: curricula lacking these formative disciplines risk producing undisciplined, 'viewy' intellects.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of instruction: cultivate method, order, system, and critical habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Impress the idea of science, method, order, principle, and system; let him start from fixed points, make his ground good as he goes, and distinguish what he knows from what he does not know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching should train students in methodical thinking and exactness rather than merely imparting miscellaneous facts; use rigorous, minute teaching and exercises that make the student active rather than passive. (Examples: critical scholarship, exercises in grammar and mathematics; anti-pattern: passive reception of images/ideas that leave no stable intellectual formation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: University education should be of sufficient duration (extended formative period)
rubrics_metrics.description: Protestants continue their studies till the age of twenty-one or twenty-two; thus they employ a time of life all-important and especially favourable to mental culture. A youth who ends his education at seventeen is no match (cæteris paribus) for one who ends it at twenty-two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should provide extended education through the key formative years (late teens into early twenties) to achieve substantial intellectual cultivation. (Policy implication: avoid truncating higher education too early; measure programs by the time allotted for formation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Against 'viewiness' and superficial extemporaneous opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of 'spurious philosophism' or 'viewiness' — the habit of being full of 'views' on all subjects without depth, produced by the demands of periodical literature and extempore journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities should guard against producing graduates who possess only shallow, flashy opinions. Emphasize depth, method, and caution over extemporaneous ‘original’ views. (Anti-patterns: rewarding rapid, topical journalism-style output as an academic virtue; tolerating flippancy and superficial generalities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: The University should cultivate sound judgment, sobriety, and self-command
rubrics_metrics.description: When the intellect has once been properly trained it will display good sense, sobriety of thought, reasonableness, candour, self-command, and steadiness of view; in some men it will lead to business habits, influence, and sagacity; in others to philosophical speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate educational outcomes by presence of practical virtues and intellectual steadiness in graduates rather than merely by acquisition of facts. (Examples: reduced inconsistency, fewer 'crotchets' or fixed irrational hobbies, greater capacity to engage difficult subjects.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities as stable, accountable institutions of authority (not anonymous literary tribunals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority which in former times was lodged in Universities now resides largely in the literary world; this is unsatisfactory because its teaching is offhand, ambitious, changeable, and often anonymous, whereas universities provide wisdom embodied in institutions that have stood the trial and are administered by men who are not anonymous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer institutional, accountable modes of intellectual authority (colleges, professorships, public lectures) over ephemeral anonymous periodical influence. Safeguard institutional continuity and public accountability as measures of quality and reliability. (Anti-pattern: letting anonymous journalists or ephemeral popularity be the arbiters of intellectual truth.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between liberal learning and professional skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge viewed in relation to professional skill: a University’s object is intellectual formation, and while professional skill has its place, the University should not be reduced to mere training for professions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a liberal curriculum that forms the intellect and not only narrowly vocational training. Professional/professional-school training can be provided elsewhere or as part of but not to the exclusion of liberal university instruction. (Scoring note: programs that are purely vocational without liberal formation fail this standard.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external (non-Catholic) learning where prudent ('Cuique in arte sua credendum')
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church has ever appealed and deferred to witnesses and authorities external to herself in matters where they have means of forming a judgment. Catholics may avail themselves of the investigations and experience of non‑Catholics in matters of education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to adopting pedagogical insights, curricular structures, and reforms observed in other (e.g., Protestant) institutions insofar as they are sound and useful. This is pragmatic guidance for building a Catholic University with competent methods. (Example: borrowing the extended age of study and disciplinary curricula that Protestants use.)
